claim: Signaling molecules derived from attachment of diverse metabolic building blocks to ascarosides play a central role in the life history of C. elegans and other nematodes.
source: Signaling molecules derived from attachment of diverse metabolic building blocks to ascarosides play a central role in the life history of C. elegans and other nematodes; however, many aspects of their biogenesis remain unclear.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established knowledge about ascarosides in nematode biology.

claim: Many aspects of ascaroside biogenesis remain unclear.
source: Signaling molecules derived from attachment of diverse metabolic building blocks to ascarosides play a central role in the life history of C. elegans and other nematodes; however, many aspects of their biogenesis remain unclear.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract acknowledging gaps in current knowledge.

claim: A pathway mediating formation of intestinal lysosome-related organelles (LROs) is required for biosynthesis of most modular ascarosides.
source: Using comparative metabolomics, we show that a pathway mediating formation of intestinal lysosome-related organelles (LROs) is required for biosynthesis of most modular ascarosides as well as previously undescribed modular glucosides.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by comparative metabolomics data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A pathway mediating formation of intestinal lysosome-related organelles (LROs) is required for biosynthesis of previously undescribed modular glucosides.
source: Using comparative metabolomics, we show that a pathway mediating formation of intestinal lysosome-related organelles (LROs) is required for biosynthesis of most modular ascarosides as well as previously undescribed modular glucosides.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by comparative metabolomics data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Modular glucosides are derived from highly selective assembly of moieties from nucleoside, amino acid, neurotransmitter, and lipid metabolism.
source: Similar to modular ascarosides, the modular glucosides are derived from highly selective assembly of moieties from nucleoside, amino acid, neurotransmitter, and lipid metabolism, suggesting that modular glucosides, like the ascarosides, may serve signaling functions.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by structural characterization and metabolomic data.

claim: Modular glucosides may serve signaling functions.
source: Similar to modular ascarosides, the modular glucosides are derived from highly selective assembly of moieties from nucleoside, amino acid, neurotransmitter, and lipid metabolism, suggesting that modular glucosides, like the ascarosides, may serve signaling functions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the structural similarity to known signaling molecules (ascarosides).

claim: Carboxylesterases that localize to intestinal organelles are required for the assembly of both modular ascarosides and glucosides via ester and amide linkages.
source: We further show that carboxylesterases that localize to intestinal organelles are required for the assembly of both modular ascarosides and glucosides via ester and amide linkages.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by genetic and metabolomic data.

claim: The metabolomes of animals may include >100,000 of compounds.
source: Recent studies indicate that the metabolomes of animals, from model systems such as Caenorhabditis elegans and Drosophila to humans, may include >100,000 of compounds (da Silva et al., 2015; Artyukhin et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The structures and functions of most small molecules in animal metabolomes have not been identified.
source: The structures and functions of most of these small molecules have not been identified, representing a largely untapped reservoir of chemical diversity and bioactivities.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Ascarosides are involved in almost every aspect of C. elegans life history, including aging, development, and behavior.
source: In C. elegans (Girard et al., 2007), a large modular library of small-molecule signals, the ascarosides, are involved in almost every aspect of its life history, including aging, development, and behavior (Schroeder, 2015; Butcher, 2017; Butcher et al., 2007; Jeong et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Ascarosides are derived from glycosides of the dideoxysugar ascarylose and hydroxylated short-chain fatty acid.
source: The ascarosides represent a structurally diverse chemical language, derived from glycosides of the dideoxysugar ascarylose and hydroxylated short-chain fatty acid (Figure 1a; von Reuss et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Structural and functional specificity of ascarosides arises from optional attachment of additional moieties to the sugar or carboxy-terminal additions to the fatty acid chain.
source: Structural and functional specificity arises from optional attachment of additional moieties to the sugar, for example indole-3-carboxylic acid (e.g. icas#3 (1)), or carboxy-terminal additions to the fatty acid chain, such as p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA, as in ascr#8 (2)) or O-glucosyl uric acid (e.g. uglas#11 (3), Figure 1b; Artyukhin et al., 2018; Artyukhin et al., 2013; Bose et al., 2014; Aprison and Ruvinsky, 2017; Curtis et al., 2020; Pungaliya et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations and reference to Figure 1b.

claim: Small changes in the chemical structures of ascarosides often result in starkly altered biological function.
source: Given that even small changes in the chemical structures of the ascarosides often result in starkly altered biological function, ascaroside biosynthesis appears to correspond to a carefully regulated encoding process in which biological state is translated into chemical structures (Panda et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Ascaroside biosynthesis corresponds to a carefully regulated encoding process in which biological state is translated into chemical structures.
source: Given that even small changes in the chemical structures of the ascarosides often result in starkly altered biological function, ascaroside biosynthesis appears to correspond to a carefully regulated encoding process in which biological state is translated into chemical structures (Panda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure-function relationship of ascarosides, supported by a citation.

claim: More than 200 C. elegans metabolites have been recently identified.
source: However, for most of the >200 recently identified C. elegans metabolites (Artyukhin et al., 2018; von Reuss et al., 2012; Artyukhin et al., 2013), biosynthetic knowledge is sparse.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Biosynthetic knowledge is sparse for most of the recently identified C. elegans metabolites.
source: However, for most of the >200 recently identified C. elegans metabolites (Artyukhin et al., 2018; von Reuss et al., 2012; Artyukhin et al., 2013), biosynthetic knowledge is sparse.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Peroxisomal β-oxidation contributes to ascaroside biosynthesis.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that conserved metabolic pathways, for example peroxisomal β-oxidation (Artyukhin et al., 2013; Bose et al., 2014) and amino acid catabolism (von Reuss et al., 2012; Srinivasan et al., 2012; Figure 1a), contribute to ascaroside biosynthesis; however, many aspects of the mechanisms underlying assembly of multi-modular metabolites remains unclear.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Amino acid catabolism contributes to ascaroside biosynthesis.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that conserved metabolic pathways, for example peroxisomal β-oxidation (Artyukhin et al., 2013; Bose et al., 2014) and amino acid catabolism (von Reuss et al., 2012; Srinivasan et al., 2012; Figure 1a), contribute to ascaroside biosynthesis; however, many aspects of the mechanisms underlying assembly of multi-modular metabolites remains unclear.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Many aspects of the mechanisms underlying assembly of multi-modular metabolites remain unclear.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that conserved metabolic pathways, for example peroxisomal β-oxidation (Artyukhin et al., 2013; Bose et al., 2014) and amino acid catabolism (von Reuss et al., 2012; Srinivasan et al., 2012; Figure 1a), contribute to ascaroside biosynthesis; however, many aspects of the mechanisms underlying assembly of multi-modular metabolites remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Metabolomic analysis of glo-1 mutants revealed complete loss of 4′-modified ascarosides.
source: Recently, metabolomic analysis of mutants of the Rab-GTPase glo-1, which lack a specific type of lysosome-related organelles (LROs, also referred to as autofluorescent gut granules), revealed complete loss of 4′-modified ascarosides (Panda et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: glo-1 mutants lack a specific type of lysosome-related organelles (LROs).
source: Recently, metabolomic analysis of mutants of the Rab-GTPase glo-1, which lack a specific type of lysosome-related organelles (LROs, also referred to as autofluorescent gut granules), revealed complete loss of 4′-modified ascarosides (Panda et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: glo-1-dependent LROs are acidic, pigmented compartments that are related to mammalian melanosomes and drosophila eye pigment organelles.
source: The glo-1-dependent LROs are acidic, pigmented compartments that are related to mammalian melanosomes and drosophila eye pigment organelles (Coburn and Gems, 2013; Hermann et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LROs form when lysosomes fuse with other cellular compartments, for example peroxisomes.
source: LROs form when lysosomes fuse with other cellular compartments, for example peroxisomes, and appear to play an important role for recycling proteins and metabolites (Coburn and Gems, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: LROs appear to play an important role for recycling proteins and metabolites.
source: LROs form when lysosomes fuse with other cellular compartments, for example peroxisomes, and appear to play an important role for recycling proteins and metabolites (Coburn and Gems, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: LROs may be involved in the production and secretion of diverse signaling molecules.
source: Additionally, it has been suggested that LROs may be involved in the production and secretion of diverse signaling molecules (Dell'Angelica et al., 2000; Luzio et al., 2014), and the observation that glo-1 mutant worms are deficient in 4′-modified ascarosides suggested that intestinal organelles may serve as hubs for their assembly (Figure 1a; Panda et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Intestinal organelles may serve as hubs for assembly of 4′-modified ascarosides.
source: Additionally, it has been suggested that LROs may be involved in the production and secretion of diverse signaling molecules (Dell'Angelica et al., 2000; Luzio et al., 2014), and the observation that glo-1 mutant worms are deficient in 4′-modified ascarosides suggested that intestinal organelles may serve as hubs for their assembly (Figure 1a; Panda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the metabolomic phenotype of glo-1 mutants, supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Several other types of intestinal granules have been characterized in C. elegans, including lipid droplets.
source: In addition to the autofluorescent LROs, several other types of intestinal granules have been characterized in C. elegans, including lipid droplets (Cao et al., 2019) and lysosome-related organelles that are not glo-1-dependent (Tanji et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Lysosome-related organelles that are not glo-1-dependent exist in C. elegans.
source: In addition to the autofluorescent LROs, several other types of intestinal granules have been characterized in C. elegans, including lipid droplets (Cao et al., 2019) and lysosome-related organelles that are not glo-1-dependent (Tanji et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Production of modular ascarosides is widely conserved among nematodes.
source: Parallel studies of other Caenorhabditis species (Dong et al., 2016; Bergame et al., 2019; Dolke et al., 2019) and Pristionchus pacificus (Falcke et al., 2018), a nematode species being developed as a satellite model system to C. elegans (Rae et al., 2008), revealed that production of modular ascarosides is widely conserved among nematodes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: uar-1 is required for 4′-attachment of an ureidoisobutyryl moiety to a subset of ascarosides in P. pacificus.
source: Leveraging the high genomic diversity of sequenced P. pacificus isolates, genome-wide association studies coupled to metabolomic analysis revealed that uar-1, a carboxylesterase from the α/ß-hydrolase superfamily with homology to cholinesterases (AChEs), is required for 4′-attachment of an ureidoisobutyryl moiety to a subset of ascarosides, e.g. ubas#3 (4, Figure 1c; Falcke et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study and reference to Figure 1c.

claim: uar-1 is a carboxylesterase from the α/ß-hydrolase superfamily with homology to cholinesterases (AChEs).
source: Leveraging the high genomic diversity of sequenced P. pacificus isolates, genome-wide association studies coupled to metabolomic analysis revealed that uar-1, a carboxylesterase from the α/ß-hydrolase superfamily with homology to cholinesterases (AChEs), is required for 4′-attachment of an ureidoisobutyryl moiety to a subset of ascarosides, e.g. ubas#3 (4, Figure 1c; Falcke et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: There is a large expansion of carboxylesterase (cest) homologs in P. pacificus and C. elegans.
source: Homology searches revealed a large expansion of carboxylesterase (cest) homologs in P. pacificus as well as C. elegans (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and recently it was shown that in C. elegans, the uar-1 homologs cest-3, cest-8, and cest-9.2 are involved in the 4′-attachment of other acyl groups in modular ascarosides (Faghih et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and a citation to a previous study.

claim: cest-3, cest-8, and cest-9.2 are involved in the 4′-attachment of other acyl groups in modular ascarosides in C. elegans.
source: Homology searches revealed a large expansion of carboxylesterase (cest) homologs in P. pacificus as well as C. elegans (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and recently it was shown that in C. elegans, the uar-1 homologs cest-3, cest-8, and cest-9.2 are involved in the 4′-attachment of other acyl groups in modular ascarosides (Faghih et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The glo-1 mutation has a dramatic impact on C. elegans metabolism.
source: These comparative analyses revealed that the glo-1 mutation has a dramatic impact on C. elegans metabolism.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by comparative metabolomics data.

claim: More than 1000 molecular features were at least 10-fold less abundant in the glo-1 exo- and endo-metabolomes in negative ionization mode.
source: For example, in negative ionization mode, we detected >1000 molecular features that were at least 10-fold less abundant in the glo-1 exo- and endo-metabolomes, as well as >3000 molecular features that are 10-fold upregulated in glo-1 mutants.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the comparative metabolomics analysis.

claim: More than 3000 molecular features are 10-fold upregulated in glo-1 mutants in negative ionization mode.
source: For example, in negative ionization mode, we detected >1000 molecular features that were at least 10-fold less abundant in the glo-1 exo- and endo-metabolomes, as well as >3000 molecular features that are 10-fold upregulated in glo-1 mutants.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the comparative metabolomics analysis.

claim: Biosynthesis of most modular ascarosides was abolished or substantially reduced in glo-1 mutants.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Panda et al., 2017), biosynthesis of most modular ascarosides was abolished or substantially reduced in glo-1 mutants, including all 4′-modified ascarosides, e.g. icas#3 (1) (Figure 1b, Figure 2—figure supplement 5a).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data and reference to figures, and is in agreement with a previous study.

claim: All 4′-modified ascarosides were abolished or substantially reduced in glo-1 mutants.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Panda et al., 2017), biosynthesis of most modular ascarosides was abolished or substantially reduced in glo-1 mutants, including all 4′-modified ascarosides, e.g. icas#3 (1) (Figure 1b, Figure 2—figure supplement 5a).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data and reference to figures.

claim: Production of ascarosides modified at the carboxy terminus was largely abolished in glo-1 mutants.
source: Similarly, production of ascarosides modified at the carboxy terminus, e.g. uglas#11 (3) derived from ester formation between ascr#1 (5) and uric acid glucoside (Curtis et al., 2020) (6), and ascr#8 (2), derived from formation of an amide bond between ascr#7 (7) and of p-amino benzoic acid (8), was largely abolished in glo-1 mutants (Figure 1a–b, Figure 2—figure supplement 5a).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data and reference to figures.

claim: Abundances of unmodified ascarosides were not significantly perturbed in glo-1 mutants.
source: For example, abundances of unmodified ascarosides, for example ascr#3 (9) and ascr#10 (10), or metabolites representing 4′-modifications, for example indole-3-carboxylic acid (11) and octopamine succinate (12), were not significantly perturbed in the mutant (Figure 1a, Figure 2—figure supplement 5a, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data and reference to figures.

claim: Metabolites representing 4′-modifications were not significantly perturbed in glo-1 mutants.
source: For example, abundances of unmodified ascarosides, for example ascr#3 (9) and ascr#10 (10), or metabolites representing 4′-modifications, for example indole-3-carboxylic acid (11) and octopamine succinate (12), were not significantly perturbed in the mutant (Figure 1a, Figure 2—figure supplement 5a, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data and reference to figures.

claim: A subset of modular ascaroside glucose esters was strongly increased in glo-1 mutants.
source: In contrast, a subset of modular ascaroside glucose esters (e.g. iglas#1 (13) and glas#10 (14), Figure 1e), was strongly increased in glo-1 mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 5b).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data and reference to figures.

claim: glo-1-dependent intestinal organelles function as a central hub for the biosynthesis of most modular ascarosides.
source: These results suggest that glo-1-dependent intestinal organelles function as a central hub for the biosynthesis of most modular ascarosides, with the exception of a subset of ascarosylated glucosides, whose increased production in glo-1 mutants may be indicative of a shunt pathway for ascarosyl-CoA derivatives (Zhang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), which represent plausible precursors for modular ascarosides modified at the carboxy terminus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the metabolomic phenotype of glo-1 mutants.

claim: Increased production of ascarosylated glucosides in glo-1 mutants may be indicative of a shunt pathway for ascarosyl-CoA derivatives.
source: These results suggest that glo-1-dependent intestinal organelles function as a central hub for the biosynthesis of most modular ascarosides, with the exception of a subset of ascarosylated glucosides, whose increased production in glo-1 mutants may be indicative of a shunt pathway for ascarosyl-CoA derivatives (Zhang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), which represent plausible precursors for modular ascarosides modified at the carboxy terminus.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the metabolomic phenotype and supported by citations.

claim: Ascarosyl-CoA derivatives represent plausible precursors for modular ascarosides modified at the carboxy terminus.
source: These results suggest that glo-1-dependent intestinal organelles function as a central hub for the biosynthesis of most modular ascarosides, with the exception of a subset of ascarosylated glucosides, whose increased production in glo-1 mutants may be indicative of a shunt pathway for ascarosyl-CoA derivatives (Zhang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), which represent plausible precursors for modular ascarosides modified at the carboxy terminus.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on biochemical reasoning and supported by citations.

claim: MS2 spectra from clusters I, II, and III suggested phosphorylated hexose glycosides of indole, anthranilic acid, tyramine, or octopamine, which are further decorated with a wide variety of fatty acyl moieties.
source: For example, MS2 spectra from clusters I, II, and III of the positive-ionization network suggested phosphorylated hexose glycosides of indole, anthranilic acid, tyramine, or octopamine, which are further decorated with a wide variety of fatty acyl moieties derived from fatty acid or amino acid metabolism, for example nicotinic acid, pyrrolic acid, or tiglic acid (Figure 2, Appendix 1—table 1; Coburn and Gems, 2013; Stupp et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a structural inference based on MS2 spectral analysis, supported by reference to figures and citations.

claim: Clusters I, II, and III represent a modular library of glucosides, in which N-glucosylated indole, anthranilic acid, tyramine, or octopamine serve as scaffolds for attachment of diverse building blocks.
source: Given the previous identification of the glucosides iglu#1/2 (15/16, Figure 2e) and angl#1/2 (17/18), we hypothesized that clusters I, II, and III represent a modular library of glucosides, in which N-glucosylated indole, anthranilic acid, tyramine, or octopamine (O'Donnell et al., 2020) serve as scaffolds for attachment of diverse building blocks.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural analysis and previous identifications, supported by reference to figures and a citation.

claim: Synthetic standards for the non-phosphorylated parent compounds of iglu#4, iglu#6, iglu#8, and iglu#10 matched HPLC retention times and MS2 spectra of the corresponding natural compounds.
source: Synthetic standards for the non-phosphorylated parent compounds of iglu#4 (19), iglu#6 (20), iglu#8 (21), and iglu#10 (22) matched HPLC retention times and MS2 spectra of the corresponding natural compounds (Figure 2—figure supplement 6), confirming their structures and enabling tentative structural assignments for a large number of additional modular glucosides, including their phosphorylated derivatives, e.g. iglu#12 (23), iglu#41 (24), angl#4 (cluster II, 25), and tyglu#4 (cluster III, 26) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by synthetic chemistry and analytical data, with reference to figures.

claim: Incorporation of tyramine and octopamine into glucosides was verified by comparison with data from a feeding experiment with stable isotope-labeled tyrosine.
source: The proposed structures include several glucosides of the neurotransmitters tyramine and octopamine, whose incorporation could be verified by comparison with data from a recently described feeding experiment with stable isotope-labeled tyrosine (O'Donnell et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by stable isotope labeling data and a citation.

claim: Production of modular glucosides is life stage dependent.
source: Similar to ascaroside biosynthesis, the production of modular glucosides is life stage dependent; for example, production of specific tyramine glucosides peaks at the L3 larval stage, whereas production of angl#4 increases until the adult stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data at different life stages, with reference to a figure.

claim: Modular glucosides were detected primarily as their phosphorylated derivatives.
source: Notably, modular glucosides were detected primarily as their phosphorylated derivatives, as respective non-phosphorylated species were generally less abundant.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on metabolomics data.

claim: Phosphorylated glucosides are more abundant in the endo-metabolome than the exo-metabolome.
source: In contrast to most ascarosides, the phosphorylated glucosides are more abundant in the endo-metabolome than the exo-metabolome, suggesting that phosphorylated glucosides may be specifically retained in the body (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data, with reference to a figure.

claim: Phosphorylated glucosides may be specifically retained in the body.
source: In contrast to most ascarosides, the phosphorylated glucosides are more abundant in the endo-metabolome than the exo-metabolome, suggesting that phosphorylated glucosides may be specifically retained in the body (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution of phosphorylated glucosides between endo- and exo-metabolomes.

claim: Abundances of putative building blocks of the newly identified modular glucosides were not strongly perturbed in glo-1 mutants.
source: As in the case of modular ascarosides, the abundances of putative building blocks of the newly identified modular glucosides were not strongly perturbed in glo-1 mutants.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data.

claim: Abundances of anthranilic acid, indole, octopamine, and tyramine were not significantly affected in glo-1 null animals.
source: For example, abundances of anthranilic acid, indole, octopamine, and tyramine were not significantly affected in glo-1 null animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data, with reference to a figure.

claim: Abundances of the glucosides scaffold, e.g. iglu#1 and angl#1, were largely unaltered or even slightly increased in glo-1 mutants.
source: Notably, abundances of the glucosides scaffold, e.g. iglu#1 and angl#1, were also largely unaltered or even slightly increased in glo-1 mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data, with reference to a figure.

claim: Production of some of the identified modular glucosides, e.g. iglu#5, is reduced but not fully abolished in glo-1 worms.
source: In addition, production of some of the identified modular glucosides, e.g. iglu#5, is reduced but not fully abolished in glo-1 worms (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data, with reference to a figure.

claim: The glo-4 metabolome closely resembles that of glo-1 worms.
source: We found that the glo-4 metabolome closely resembles that of glo-1 worms, lacking most of the modular ascarosides and ascarosides detected in wildtype worms (Figure 2—figure supplement 5c).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by comparative metabolomics data, with reference to a figure.

claim: glo-4 encodes a predicted guanyl-nucleotide exchange factor acting upstream of glo-1.
source: glo-4 encodes a predicted guanyl-nucleotide exchange factor acting upstream of glo-1, and like glo-1 mutants, glo-4 worms do not form LROs (Hermann et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: glo-4 worms do not form LROs.
source: glo-4 encodes a predicted guanyl-nucleotide exchange factor acting upstream of glo-1, and like glo-1 mutants, glo-4 worms do not form LROs (Hermann et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Similar sets of compounds are upregulated in glo-1 and glo-4 mutants relative to wild type, including ascarosyl glucosides and ascaroside phosphates.
source: Correspondingly, similar sets of compounds are upregulated in glo-1 and glo-4 mutants relative to wild type, including ascarosyl glucosides and ascaroside phosphates.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by comparative metabolomics data.

claim: Compounds accumulating in glo-1 and glo-4 mutant worms include a diverse array of small peptides (primarily three to six amino acids).
source: Compounds accumulating in glo-1 and glo-4 mutant worms further include a diverse array of small peptides (primarily three to six amino acids), consistent with the proposed role of LROs in the breakdown of peptides derived from proteolysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 10; Bird et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data, with reference to a figure and a citation.

claim: LROs serve as hotspots of biosynthetic activity, where building blocks from diverse metabolic pathways are attached to glucoside and ascaroside scaffolds.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that, in addition to their roles in the degradation of metabolic waste, the LROs serve as hotspots of biosynthetic activity, where building blocks from diverse metabolic pathways are attached to glucoside and ascaroside scaffolds (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on the metabolomic phenotypes of glo-1 and glo-4 mutants, with reference to a figure.

claim: Combinations of different building blocks and scaffolds in modular glucosides and ascarosides are highly specific.
source: Comparing the relative abundances of different members of the identified families of modular glucosides and ascarosides, it appears that combinations of different building blocks and scaffolds are highly specific, suggesting the presence of dedicated biosynthetic pathways.
evidence: This is an observation from the study based on metabolomics data.

claim: Uric acid glucoside is preferentially combined with an ascaroside bearing a seven-carbon side chain.
source: For example, uric acid glucoside, gluric#1 (6), is preferentially combined with an ascaroside bearing a seven-carbon side chain (to form uglas#11, 3), whereas ascarosides bearing a nine-carbon side chain are preferentially attached to the anomeric position of free glucose, as in glas#10 (14) (Artyukhin et al., 2018; von Reuss et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an observation from the study supported by metabolomics data and citations.

claim: Ascarosides bearing a nine-carbon side chain are preferentially attached to the anomeric position of free glucose.
source: For example, uric acid glucoside, gluric#1 (6), is preferentially combined with an ascaroside bearing a seven-carbon side chain (to form uglas#11, 3), whereas ascarosides bearing a nine-carbon side chain are preferentially attached to the anomeric position of free glucose, as in glas#10 (14) (Artyukhin et al., 2018; von Reuss et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an observation from the study supported by metabolomics data and citations.

claim: Tiglic acid is preferentially attached to indole and tyramine glucosides but not to anthranilic acid glucosides.
source: Similarly, tiglic acid is preferentially attached to indole and tyramine glucosides but not to anthranilic acid glucosides (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the study based on metabolomics data.

claim: The biosynthesis of other modular ascarosides as well as the newly identified glucosides may be under the control of cest family enzymes.
source: Given that 4′-modification of ascarosides in P. pacificus and C. elegans require cest homologs, we hypothesized that the biosynthesis of other modular ascarosides as well as the newly identified glucosides may be under the control of cest family enzymes (Falcke et al., 2018; Faghih et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous findings about cest homologs, supported by citations.

claim: Two of the seven tested cest homologs (cest-1.1, cest-2.2) are defective in the production of two different families of modular ascarosides.
source: We found that two of the seven tested homologs (cest-1.1, cest-2.2) are defective in the production of two different families of modular ascarosides, whereas cest-4 mutants were defective in the biosynthesis of a specific subset of modular indole glucosides (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data of cest mutants, with reference to a figure.

claim: cest-4 mutants were defective in the biosynthesis of a specific subset of modular indole glucosides.
source: We found that two of the seven tested homologs (cest-1.1, cest-2.2) are defective in the production of two different families of modular ascarosides, whereas cest-4 mutants were defective in the biosynthesis of a specific subset of modular indole glucosides (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data of cest mutants, with reference to a figure.

claim: The metabolomes of mutants for the remaining four cest homologs did not exhibit any significant differences compared to wild type under the tested conditions.
source: The metabolomes of mutants for the remaining four cest homologs did not exhibit any significant differences compared to wild type under the tested conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on metabolomics data of cest mutants.

claim: Production of ascr#8, ascr#81, and ascr#82 is abolished in cest-2.2 mutants.
source: Analysis of the metabolomes of the two cest-2.2 null mutants revealed loss of dauer pheromone component and male attractant ascr#8 (2) as well as of the closely related ascr#81 (27) and ascr#82 (28) (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2b).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data of cest-2.2 mutants, with reference to figures.

claim: The ascr#8 family of ascarosides are derived from amide formation between ascr#7 and folate-derived p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA), PABA-glutamate, or PABA-diglutamate.
source: Biosynthetically, the ascr#8 family of ascarosides are derived from amide formation between ascr#7 (ΔC7, 7) and folate-derived p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA, 8), PABA-glutamate (29), or PABA-diglutamate, respectively.
evidence: This is a statement about the biosynthetic pathway based on established knowledge.

claim: No significant reduction in the production of plausible ascr#8 precursors, including PABA and PABA-glutamate, or ascr#7 was detected in cest-2.2 mutants.
source: We did not detect any significant reduction in the production of plausible ascr#8 precursors, including PABA and PABA-glutamate, or ascr#7 (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data of cest-2.2 mutants, with reference to figures.

claim: Biosynthesis of ascr#8, ascr#81, and ascr#82 was recovered in cest-2.2 mutant worms in which the cest-2.2 sequence had been restored to wild type using CRISPR/Cas9.
source: Biosynthesis of ascr#8, ascr#81, and ascr#82 was recovered in cest-2.2 mutant worms in which the cest-2.2 sequence had been restored to wild type using CRISPR/Cas9 (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data of genetic revertants, with reference to figures.

claim: CEST-2.2 is required specifically for biosynthesis of the amide linkage between the carboxy terminus of ascr#7 and PABA derivatives.
source: These results indicate that CEST-2.2 is required specifically for biosynthesis of the amide linkage between the carboxy terminus of ascr#7 and PABA derivatives, in contrast to the implied functions of UAR-1, CEST-8, CEST-3, and CEST-9.2, which are involved in the formation of ester bonds between various head groups and the 4′-hydroxy group of ascarylose (Falcke et al., 2018; Faghih et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on the metabolomic phenotype of cest-2.2 mutants and revertants, supported by citations.

claim: Biosynthesis of uglas#1 and uglas#11 was abolished in cest-1.1 null mutants.
source: In cest-1.1 null mutants (cest-1.1(null)), biosynthesis of the nucleoside-like ascaroside uglas#1 (30) and its phosphorylated derivative uglas#11 (3) was abolished (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data of cest-1.1 mutants, with reference to figures.

claim: uglas#1 and uglas#11 are derived from the attachment of ascr#1 to the uric acid gluconucleoside gluric#1.
source: uglas#1 and uglas#11 are derived from the attachment of ascr#1, bearing a seven carbon (C7) side chain, to the uric acid gluconucleoside gluric#1 (6).
evidence: This is a statement about the biosynthetic pathway based on structural analysis.

claim: Production of ascr#1 and gluric#1 was not reduced in cest-1.1 null mutants.
source: Production of ascr#1 (5) and gluric#1 (6), representing plausible building blocks of uglas#1 (30), was not reduced (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data of cest-1.1 mutants, with reference to a figure.

claim: Production of uglas#14 and uglas#15 was not abolished but rather slightly increased in cest-1.1(null).
source: Furthermore, production of uglas#14 (31) and uglas#15 (32), isomers of uglas#1 and uglas#11 bearing the ascarosyl moiety at the 6′ position instead of the 2′ position, was not abolished but rather slightly increased in cest-1.1(null) (Figure 3d–e).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data of cest-1.1 mutants, with reference to figures.

claim: CEST-1.1 is required for the formation of the ester bond specifically between ascr#1 and the 2′-hydroxyl group in gluric#1.
source: These results indicate that CEST-1.1 is required for the formation of the ester bond specifically between ascr#1 (5) and the 2′-hydroxyl group in gluric#1.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on the metabolomic phenotype of cest-1.1 mutants.

claim: Biosynthesis of uglas#1 and uglas#11 was fully recovered in cest-1.1 mutant worms in which the cest-1.1 sequence had been restored to wild type using CRISPR/Cas9.
source: As in the case of cest-2.2, biosynthesis of uglas#1 and uglas#11 was fully recovered in cest-1.1 mutant worms in which the cest-1.1 sequence had been restored to wild type using CRISPR/Cas9 (Figure 3f, Figure 3—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data of genetic revertants, with reference to figures.

claim: Serine 213 is part of the conserved catalytic serine-histidine-glutamate triad of CEST-1.1.
source: Sequence alignment with human AChE suggested that serine 213 is part of the conserved catalytic serine-histidine-glutamate triad of CEST-1.1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence alignment, with reference to a figure.

claim: Production of uglas#1 and uglas#11 was fully abolished in cest-1.1(S213A).
source: As in cest-1.1(null), production of uglas#1 (30) and uglas#11 (3) was fully abolished in cest-1.1(S213A), whereas production of gluric#1 was not affected (Figure 3g).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data of the cest-1.1(S213A) mutant, with reference to a figure.

claim: Production of gluric#1 was not affected in cest-1.1(S213A).
source: As in cest-1.1(null), production of uglas#1 (30) and uglas#11 (3) was fully abolished in cest-1.1(S213A), whereas production of gluric#1 was not affected (Figure 3g).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data of the cest-1.1(S213A) mutant, with reference to a figure.

claim: cest-1.1 is implicated with longevity phenotypes associated with argonaute-like gene 2 (alg-2).
source: Previous work implicated cest-1.1 with longevity phenotypes associated with argonaute-like gene 2 (alg-2) (Aalto et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: alg-2 mutant worms are long lived compared to wild type.
source: alg-2 mutant worms are long lived compared to wild type and their long lifespan was further shown to require daf-16, the sole ortholog of the FOXO family of transcription factors in C. elegans, as well as cest-1.1.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: The long lifespan of alg-2 mutants requires daf-16 and cest-1.1.
source: alg-2 mutant worms are long lived compared to wild type and their long lifespan was further shown to require daf-16, the sole ortholog of the FOXO family of transcription factors in C. elegans, as well as cest-1.1.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: uglas#11 biosynthesis is significantly increased in mutants of the insulin receptor homolog daf-2.
source: Moreover, uglas#11 biosynthesis is significantly increased in mutants of the insulin receptor homolog daf-2, a central regulator of lifespan in C. elegans upstream of daf-16 (Curtis et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The production of uglas ascarosides may underlie the cest-1.1-dependent extension of adult lifespan in C. elegans.
source: These findings suggest the possibility that the production of uglas ascarosides underlies the cest-1.1-dependent extension of adult lifespan in C. elegans.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the connection between cest-1.1, uglas ascarosides, and longevity pathways.

claim: The levels of iglu#3 and its phosphorylated derivative iglu#4 were abolished in the cest-4 mutant worms.
source: Instead, we found that the levels of a specific subset of modular anthranilic acid (33) bearing indole glucosides, including iglu#3 (34) and its phosphorylated derivative iglu#4 (35) were abolished in the cest-4 mutant worms (Figure 3h).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data of cest-4 mutants, with reference to a figure.

claim: Abundances of the putative precursor glucosides, iglu#1 and iglu#2, were not significantly changed in cest-4.
source: Abundances of the putative precursor glucosides, iglu#1 (15) and iglu#2 (16), were not significantly changed in cest-4 (Figure 3i, Figure 3—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data of cest-4 mutants, with reference to figures.

claim: Production of other indole glucosides, e.g. iglu#6 and iglu#8, was not significantly reduced in cest-4 worms.
source: Notably, production of other indole glucosides, e.g. iglu#6 (36) and iglu#8 (37), was not significantly reduced in cest-4 worms (Figure 3j, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data of cest-4 mutants, with reference to figures.

claim: Biosynthesis of iglu#3 and iglu#4 was restored to wild-type levels in genetic revertant strains for cest-4.
source: Biosynthesis of iglu#3 and iglu#4 was restored to wild-type levels in genetic revertant strains for cest-4 (Figure 3i, Figure 3—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data of genetic revertants, with reference to figures.

claim: cest-4 is specifically required for attachment of anthranilic acid to the 6′ position of glucosyl indole precursors.
source: Therefore, it appears that cest-4 is specifically required for attachment of anthranilic acid to the 6′ position of glucosyl indole precursors, whereas attachment of tiglic acid, nicotinic acid, and other moieties is cest-4-independent (Figure 3j, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on the metabolomic phenotype of cest-4 mutants, with reference to figures.

claim: Attachment of tiglic acid, nicotinic acid, and other moieties to indole glucosides is cest-4-independent.
source: Therefore, it appears that cest-4 is specifically required for attachment of anthranilic acid to the 6′ position of glucosyl indole precursors, whereas attachment of tiglic acid, nicotinic acid, and other moieties is cest-4-independent (Figure 3j, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on the metabolomic phenotype of cest-4 mutants, with reference to figures.

claim: All cest homologs selected for this study exhibit domain architectures typical of the α/ß-hydrolase superfamily of proteins, including a conserved catalytic triad.
source: All cest homologs selected for this study exhibit domain architectures typical of the α/ß-hydrolase superfamily of proteins, including a conserved catalytic triad, and further contain a predicted disulfide bridge, as in mammalian AChE (Soreq and Seidman, 2001; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis, supported by a citation and reference to a figure.

claim: The cest genes contain a predicted disulfide bridge, as in mammalian AChE.
source: All cest homologs selected for this study exhibit domain architectures typical of the α/ß-hydrolase superfamily of proteins, including a conserved catalytic triad, and further contain a predicted disulfide bridge, as in mammalian AChE (Soreq and Seidman, 2001; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis, supported by a citation and reference to a figure.

claim: The cest genes share homology with neuroligin.
source: The cest genes also share homology with neuroligin, a membrane bound member of the α/ß-hydrolase fold family, that mediates the formation and maintenance of synapses between neurons (Bemben et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Five of the seven CEST homologs studied are membrane anchored, with a predicted C-terminal transmembrane domain.
source: Sequence analysis suggests that five of the seven CEST homologs studied here are membrane anchored, given the presence of a predicted C-terminal transmembrane domain (Krogh et al., 2001) (consisting of ~20 residues), with the N terminus on the luminal side of a vesicle or organelle (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis, supported by a citation and reference to a figure.

claim: Production of all cest-2.2-dependent metabolites was not significantly altered in cest-2.2-mCherry mutants.
source: We confirmed that production of all cest-2.2-dependent metabolites, including ascr#8 (2), ascr#81 (27), and ascr#82 (28) was not significantly altered in cest-2.2-mCherry mutants (Figure 4a), indicating that CEST-2.2 remained functional.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data of the tagged strain, with reference to a figure.

claim: CEST-2.2-mCherry localizes to a subset of intestinal organelles that is partly distinct from the autofluorescent LROs.
source: In addition, cest-2.2-mCherry-tagged worms showed red fluorescence in a distinct set of intestinal granules that showed little if any autofluorescence (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplements 3–4). It is unclear whether mCherry also localizes to the strongly autofluorescent granules, as we cannot distinguish the mCherry signal from the red component of the autofluorescence, given relatively low CEST-2.2-mCherry expression in this non-overexpressing strain. Taken together, it appears that CEST-2.2-mCherry localizes to a subset of intestinal organelles that is partly distinct from the autofluorescent LROs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by imaging data, with reference to figures.

claim: Biosynthesis of all known modular ascarosides is abolished in Cbr-glo-1 worms.
source: Comparative metabolomic analysis of the endo- and exo-metabolomes of wild-type C. briggsae and the Cbr-glo-1 mutant strains revealed that biosynthesis of all known modular ascarosides is abolished in Cbr-glo-1 worms, including the indole carboxy derivatives icas#2 (35) and icas#6.2 (36), which are highly abundant in wild-type C. briggsae (Figure 5a; Dong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by comparative metabolomics data of C. briggsae mutants, with reference to a figure and a citation.

claim: The C. briggsae MS2 networks included several large Cbr-glo-1-dependent clusters representing modular glucosides.
source: In addition, the C. briggsae MS2 networks included several large Cbr-glo-1-dependent clusters representing modular glucosides, including many of the compounds also detected in C. elegans, for example iglu#4 and angl#4.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by MS2 network analysis of C. briggsae metabolomes.

claim: Production of unmodified glucoside scaffolds, e.g. iglu#1 and angl#1, was not reduced or increased in Cbr-glo-1 mutants.
source: As in C. elegans, production of unmodified glucoside scaffolds, e.g. iglu#1 (15) and angl#1 (17), was not reduced or increased in Cbr-glo-1 mutants, whereas biosynthesis of most modular glucosides derived from attachment of additional moieties to these scaffolds was abolished (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data of C. briggsae mutants, with reference to a figure.

claim: Biosynthesis of most modular glucosides derived from attachment of additional moieties to glucoside scaffolds was abolished in Cbr-glo-1 mutants.
source: As in C. elegans, production of unmodified glucoside scaffolds, e.g. iglu#1 (15) and angl#1 (17), was not reduced or increased in Cbr-glo-1 mutants, whereas biosynthesis of most modular glucosides derived from attachment of additional moieties to these scaffolds was abolished (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data of C. briggsae mutants, with reference to a figure.

claim: The role of LROs as a central hub for the assembly of diverse small molecule architectures may be widely conserved among nematodes.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the role of LROs as a central hub for the assembly of diverse small molecule architectures, including modular glucosides and ascarosides, may be widely conserved among nematodes (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on the conservation of the glo-1 phenotype in C. briggsae, with reference to a figure.

claim: glo-1 is required for formation of intestinal LROs and plays a central role in the biosynthesis of several large compound families derived from modular assembly via cest homologs.
source: Our results indicate that in C. elegans the Rab-GTPase glo-1, which is required for formation of intestinal LROs, plays a central role in the biosynthesis of several large compound families derived from modular assembly via cest homologs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study based on the metabolomic phenotypes of glo-1 mutants and cest mutants.

claim: Formation of the autofluorescent LROs via glo-1 is reminiscent of the roles of its human orthologs RAB32 and RAB38.
source: Formation of the autofluorescent LROs via glo-1 is reminiscent of the roles of its human orthologs RAB32 and RAB38, which are required for the formation of melanosomes, and perhaps other LROs (Wasmeier et al., 2006; Marks et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RAB32 and RAB38 are required for the formation of melanosomes.
source: Formation of the autofluorescent LROs via glo-1 is reminiscent of the roles of its human orthologs RAB32 and RAB38, which are required for the formation of melanosomes, and perhaps other LROs (Wasmeier et al., 2006; Marks et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Lysosomes and LROs are generally presumed to function in autophagy, phagocytosis, and the hydrolytic degradation of proteins.
source: Lysosomes and LROs are generally presumed to function in autophagy, phagocytosis, and the hydrolytic degradation of proteins, and Rab32 family GTPases have been shown to be required for these processes in diverse organisms (Morris et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Rab32 family GTPases have been shown to be required for autophagy, phagocytosis, and the hydrolytic degradation of proteins in diverse organisms.
source: Lysosomes and LROs are generally presumed to function in autophagy, phagocytosis, and the hydrolytic degradation of proteins, and Rab32 family GTPases have been shown to be required for these processes in diverse organisms (Morris et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Many of the building blocks of the identified modular ascarosides and glucosides are derived from catabolic pathways.
source: Consistent with the notion that lysosomes and LROs are degradation hotspots, many of the building blocks of the identified modular ascarosides and glucosides are derived from catabolic pathways, for example, anthranilic acid is derived from tryptophan catabolism, uric acid stems from purine metabolism, and the short chain ascarosides are the end products of peroxisomal β-oxidation of very long-chain precursors.
evidence: This is an observation from the study based on the identified structures and known metabolic pathways.

claim: Anthranilic acid is derived from tryptophan catabolism.
source: Consistent with the notion that lysosomes and LROs are degradation hotspots, many of the building blocks of the identified modular ascarosides and glucosides are derived from catabolic pathways, for example, anthranilic acid is derived from tryptophan catabolism, uric acid stems from purine metabolism, and the short chain ascarosides are the end products of peroxisomal β-oxidation of very long-chain precursors.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Uric acid stems from purine metabolism.
source: Consistent with the notion that lysosomes and LROs are degradation hotspots, many of the building blocks of the identified modular ascarosides and glucosides are derived from catabolic pathways, for example, anthranilic acid is derived from tryptophan catabolism, uric acid stems from purine metabolism, and the short chain ascarosides are the end products of peroxisomal β-oxidation of very long-chain precursors.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: The short chain ascarosides are the end products of peroxisomal β-oxidation of very long-chain precursors.
source: Consistent with the notion that lysosomes and LROs are degradation hotspots, many of the building blocks of the identified modular ascarosides and glucosides are derived from catabolic pathways, for example, anthranilic acid is derived from tryptophan catabolism, uric acid stems from purine metabolism, and the short chain ascarosides are the end products of peroxisomal β-oxidation of very long-chain precursors.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: The modular assembly paradigm extends beyond ascarosides.
source: Further, our results demonstrate that the modular assembly paradigm extends beyond ascarosides.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on the discovery of modular glucosides.

claim: The modular glucosides represent a previously unknown family of nematode metabolites.
source: The modular glucosides represent a previously unknown family of nematode metabolites.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Some modular glucosides are excreted into the media.
source: Like the ascaroside pheromones, some modular glucosides are excreted into the media, suggesting that they could be involved in inter-organismal communication.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on metabolomics data.

claim: Some modular glucosides could be involved in inter-organismal communication.
source: Like the ascaroside pheromones, some modular glucosides are excreted into the media, suggesting that they could be involved in inter-organismal communication.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation that some modular glucosides are excreted.

claim: The apparent peroxisomal origin of the ascaroside scaffolds suggests a link between peroxisome and gut granule activity, perhaps via pexophagy.
source: In particular, the apparent peroxisomal origin of the ascaroside scaffolds suggests a link between peroxisome and gut granule activity, perhaps via pexophagy (Sakai et al., 2006), and characterization of the role of autophagy for gut granule-dependent metabolism may contribute to uncovering the functions of modular glucoside and ascarosides.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the known biosynthetic origins of ascarosides, supported by a citation.

claim: A connection to autophagy is suggested by the finding that production of modular ascarosides is reduced in mutants of atg-18.
source: A connection to autophagy is also suggested by our previous finding (Panda et al., 2017) that production of modular ascarosides is reduced in mutants of atg-18 (Palmisano and Meléndez, 2019), which is essential for autophagy.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: atg-18 is essential for autophagy.
source: A connection to autophagy is also suggested by our previous finding (Panda et al., 2017) that production of modular ascarosides is reduced in mutants of atg-18 (Palmisano and Meléndez, 2019), which is essential for autophagy.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The high degree of selectivity in which different building blocks are combined in the modular ascarosides and glucosides strongly suggests that these compounds represent products of dedicated enzymatic pathways.
source: The high degree of selectivity in which different building blocks are combined in the modular ascarosides and glucosides strongly suggests that these compounds, despite their numbers and diversity, represent products of dedicated enzymatic pathways, as has recently been established for 4′-acylated ascarosides.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed selectivity in modular metabolite assembly.

claim: cest homologs are associated with a wider range of biosynthetic functions, including esterification and amide formation at the carboxy terminus of ascarosides and acylation of glucosides.
source: Our results revealed a wider range of biosynthetic functions associated with cest homologs, including esterification and amide formation at the carboxy terminus of ascarosides and acylation of glucosides (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on the metabolomic phenotypes of cest mutants, with reference to a figure.

claim: All cest null mutants whose metabolomes have been characterized so far are defective in the biosynthesis of one or a few compounds sharing a specific structural feature.
source: Notably, all cest null mutants whose metabolomes have been characterized so far are defective in the biosynthesis of one or a few compounds sharing a specific structural feature, further supporting the view that these selectively assembled molecular architectures serve dedicated functions.
evidence: This is an observation from the study based on the metabolomic phenotypes of cest mutants.

claim: All CEST proteins that have been associated with modular metabolite assembly contain membrane-anchors.
source: All CEST proteins that so far have been associated with modular metabolite assembly contain membrane-anchors and exhibit domain architectures typical of serine hydrolases of the AChE family, including an α/β-hydrolase fold, a conserved catalytic serine-histidine-glutamate triad, and bridging disulfide cysteines (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Soreq and Seidman, 2001).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis, supported by a citation and reference to a figure.

claim: CEST proteins exhibit domain architectures typical of serine hydrolases of the AChE family.
source: All CEST proteins that so far have been associated with modular metabolite assembly contain membrane-anchors and exhibit domain architectures typical of serine hydrolases of the AChE family, including an α/β-hydrolase fold, a conserved catalytic serine-histidine-glutamate triad, and bridging disulfide cysteines (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Soreq and Seidman, 2001).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis, supported by a citation and reference to a figure.

claim: Mutation of the catalytic serine in cest-1.1(S213A) abolished production of all cest-1.1-dependent compounds.
source: While our efforts at heterologous expression of CEST proteins were unsuccessful, the finding that mutation of the catalytic serine in cest-1.1(S213A) abolished production of all cest-1.1-dependent compounds suggests that CEST enzymes directly participate in the biosynthesis of modular metabolites.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by metabolomics data of the cest-1.1(S213A) mutant.

claim: CEST enzymes directly participate in the biosynthesis of modular metabolites.
source: While our efforts at heterologous expression of CEST proteins were unsuccessful, the finding that mutation of the catalytic serine in cest-1.1(S213A) abolished production of all cest-1.1-dependent compounds suggests that CEST enzymes directly participate in the biosynthesis of modular metabolites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effect of the catalytic serine mutation.

claim: CEST proteins partake in the assembly of diverse ascaroside or glucoside-based architectures via acyl transfer from corresponding activated intermediates, e.g. CoA or phosphate esters.
source: Therefore, we hypothesize that CEST proteins, after translating from the endomembrane system to glo-1-dependent intestinal organelles, partake in the assembly of diverse ascaroside or glucoside-based architectures via acyl transfer from corresponding activated intermediates, e.g. CoA or phosphate esters (Soreq and Seidman, 2001; Vaz and Wanders, 2002).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the enzymatic properties of CEST proteins and supported by citations.

claim: α/β-hydrolase fold enzymes are functionally highly diverse.
source: α/β-hydrolase fold enzymes are functionally highly diverse (Rauwerdink and Kazlauskas, 2015) and include esterases, peptidases, oxidoreductases, and lyases, serving diverse biosynthetic roles in animals, plants (Mindrebo et al., 2016), and bacteria (Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: α/β-hydrolase fold enzymes can function as dedicated acyltransferases.
source: While acyltransferase activity is often observed as a side reaction for esterases and lipases, α/β-hydrolase fold enzymes can function as dedicated acyltransferases, for example in microbial natural product biosyntheses (Rauwerdink and Kazlauskas, 2015; Lejon et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some modular ascarosides, e.g. iglas#1, do not appear to be glo-1-dependent.
source: Finally, although our results indicate that glo-1 is required for the biosynthesis of most modular metabolites we have detected so far, it is notable that some modular ascarosides, e.g. iglas#1 (13), and modular glucosides, e.g. iglu#6 (20) and iglu#8 (21), do not appear to be glo-1-dependent (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on metabolomics data, with reference to a figure.

claim: Some modular glucosides, e.g. iglu#6 and iglu#8, do not appear to be glo-1-dependent.
source: Finally, although our results indicate that glo-1 is required for the biosynthesis of most modular metabolites we have detected so far, it is notable that some modular ascarosides, e.g. iglas#1 (13), and modular glucosides, e.g. iglu#6 (20) and iglu#8 (21), do not appear to be glo-1-dependent (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on metabolomics data, with reference to a figure.

claim: Diverse cell compartments contribute to modular metabolite biosynthesis.
source: This suggests that diverse cell compartments contribute to modular metabolite biosynthesis and may also indicate that not all CEST proteins are delivered to the same cellular compartment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that some modular metabolites are not glo-1-dependent.

claim: Not all CEST proteins may be delivered to the same cellular compartment.
source: This suggests that diverse cell compartments contribute to modular metabolite biosynthesis and may also indicate that not all CEST proteins are delivered to the same cellular compartment.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation that some modular metabolites are not glo-1-dependent.

claim: glo-1 mutants continue to generate the simple glucosides and ascarosides that serve as scaffolds for further elaboration via CEST proteins.
source: Similarly, glo-1 mutants continue to generate the simple glucosides and ascarosides that serve as scaffolds for further elaboration via CEST proteins, which may be derived from UDP-glycosyltransferases (Mackenzie et al., 2005).
